passages.t: A lament for Pharaoh, the monster in the seas
passages.happening:
In the twelfth year God tells Ezekiel to lament for Pharaoh: ‘You are like a lion among the nations; you are like a monster in the seas. You thrash about in your rivers, churning up the waters with your feet and muddying the streams’ (verse 2). God will throw his net over him, haul him out and leave him on the land for the birds and beasts (verses 3-6).

‘When I extinguish you, I will cover the heavens and darken their stars’ (verse 7); sun and moon will give no light over his land (verses 7-8). The sword of the king of Babylon will come against Egypt (verse 11). Its people will be struck down, its waters will settle, and the daughters of the nations will chant this lament over Egypt (verses 12-16).
passages.hearers:
The first oracle is dated to about March 585 BC. Pharaoh Hophra still ruled Egypt, and verse 11 names the agent plainly: the king of Babylon.

The monster translates a word used for great sea or river creatures and sometimes for the chaos dragon of ancient myth. For Egypt it suggests the Nile crocodile, linked in Egyptian religion with royal power. In older Near Eastern stories a god captures a chaos beast in a net; here the monster is only a king, and Israel's God catches him easily. The darkening of the sun would strike hard in Egypt, where the sun god was central to royal ideology.
passages.later: At the exodus, darkness fell over the land of Egypt (Exodus 10:21-22). Isaiah pictured Sheol stirring to meet a fallen king (Isaiah 14:9).
passages.asks: Pharaoh thrashed about and muddied the waters. Ask where your restlessness stirs up trouble for others. And ask what quietness before God would look like.

passages.happening:
‘Son of man, wail for the multitudes of Egypt’ (verse 18), and send her down to the depths of the earth with those who go down to the Pit. Mighty chiefs in Sheol will say that Egypt and her allies ‘have come down and lie with the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword’ (verse 21).

The poem calls the roll of fallen nations lying there with their graves around them: Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north and the Sidonians, each of whom once spread terror in the land of the living (verses 22-30). ‘Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude’ (verse 31); he too will lie among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
These were real powers from Israel's recent memory. Assyria had fallen in the late seventh century BC. Elam, east of Babylonia, was laid waste by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in the middle of that century. Meshech and Tubal were peoples of Anatolia, remembered as fierce warriors. Edom was Judah's neighbor to the southeast.

A proper grave with one's weapons and honors mattered deeply. The mighty warriors of old in verse 27 lie with their swords under their heads, a picture of honorable burial. The nations of this chapter lie in shame. Pharaoh's comfort is bitter: he is not alone in his fall.
passages.later: Isaiah heard the dead kings say to the fallen king of Babylon, ‘You too have become weak, as we are’ (Isaiah 14:10). Daniel later speaks of those who sleep in the dust awakening (Daniel 12:2).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter teach what the afterlife is like?

It is better read as a poetic taunt than as a map of the afterlife. Ezekiel uses the common Israelite picture of Sheol as a shadowy realm below the earth where the dead lie together, and he arranges the nations in it for effect: the honored and the dishonored, the circumcised and the uncircumcised, each nation's graves around it. Some interpreters see in the difference between the honored warriors of verse 27 and the shamed nations an early sign of a developing picture of the dead. Others caution that the distinctions concern honor in burial and memory, not reward and punishment after death. The fuller hope of resurrection comes later in the Old Testament, in Daniel 12:2, and is central in the New. The chapter should not be pressed for details it never set out to give.
passages.asks: Every great power on the roll once spread terror and now lies still. Ask what you fear in the world around you. And ask what it means that God outlasts every power.
